A cellular network is composed of a large number of cells, each consisting of a cluster of base stations, also known as cell towers or cell sites. Each cell has its own unique identifier, and the base stations transmit and receive radio signals to and from mobile devices within that cell.

3. The MSC connects the mobile device to the Public Switched Telephone Network (PSTN) or the internet, allowing users to make voice calls, send text messages, and access data services such as email, web browsing, and online applications.
4. The MSC also coordinates the handover of the mobile device from one cell to another when the device moves out of range of the original cell.

Cellular networks use a variety of technologies to manage the airflow of voice and data traffic, including:

2. Time Division Multiple Access (TDMA): assigns a specific time slot to each user for transmitting and receiving data.
3. Code Division Multiple Access (CDMA): uses unique codes to identify and separate the signals of multiple users.
4. Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiple Access (OFDMA): combines the benefits of FDMA and TDMA to improve data transmission efficiency.

There are two main types of cellular networks:
